Quartus
KWOR-tus
proper noun (figure)
Latin Quartus ("fourth"), a common Roman name often given to a fourth child or fourth-born. One of the brethren who sent greetings in Paul's letter to the Romans (Rom 16:23).

Biblical Definition

Quartus is a Christian brother at Corinth named in a single line of Scripture — the closing greetings of Paul's epistle to the Romans: "Gaius mine host, and of the whole church, saluteth you. Erastus the chamberlain of the city saluteth you, and Quartus a brother" (Rom 16:23). Of Quartus we know nothing beyond his name and that one designation: "a brother." His Latin name ("fourth") suggests he may have been a Roman, perhaps of servile origin (such ordinal names were common among slaves and freedmen). Yet the Spirit of God saw fit to preserve his name and his greeting in the inspired and permanent Word of God, alongside the more prominent Gaius and Erastus. That is the quiet dignity of Quartus: an obscure believer of no recorded office, no recorded deed, no recorded word — remembered forever in Scripture simply as "a brother." He stands for the great multitude of ordinary, faithful, unremarkable Christians whose names are written not chiefly in the few verses of Scripture but in the Lamb's book of life (Rev 21:27), and whose simple designation — brother, sister, member of the family of God — is honor enough. The naming of Quartus reminds the church that God's record is not the world's record: the world remembers the great, but the Spirit remembered "Quartus a brother," and that remembrance will outlast every monument of the mighty.

Webster 1828 Definition

A Christian brother at Corinth named once in Scripture, in the closing greetings of Romans (Rom 16:23), simply as "a brother"; he stands for the great multitude of obscure, faithful believers whose dignity is their brotherhood in Christ.

QUARTUS, proper noun. Latin Quartus ("fourth"); a common Roman ordinal name, often of slaves or freedmen.

A Christian brother at Corinth, named once in Scripture: Rom 16:23, in the closing greetings of Romans.

Described simply as "Quartus a brother"; nothing else is recorded of him.

Stands for the great multitude of ordinary, faithful believers remembered in the Lamb's book of life.

His naming shows that God's record differs from the world's: the Spirit preserved "a brother."

Key Scripture

Romans 16:23 — "Gaius mine host, and of the whole church, saluteth you. Erastus the chamberlain of the city saluteth you, and Quartus a brother."

Revelation 21:27 — "And there shall in no wise enter into it any thing that defileth... but they which are written in the Lamb's book of life."

Matthew 12:50 — "For whosoever shall do the will of my Father which is in heaven, the same is my brother, and sister, and mother."

Malachi 3:16 — "Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD."

Modern Corruption

Quartus is corrupted only when his obscurity is despised — when the church values the named and prominent and forgets that the Spirit honored an unknown believer simply as "a brother."

expand to see more

Obscurity-despised. The world, and too often the church, prizes the prominent, the gifted, the named, and overlooks the obscure faithful. The single line that preserves Quartus is a rebuke to that instinct: the Spirit of God, inspiring the most theologically weighty letter in the New Testament, paused to record the greeting of a man we know only as "a brother." His brotherhood in Christ was honor enough to be written in the permanent Word. The church that learns from Quartus learns to honor the ordinary faithful member as God honors him — not for office or fame, but for being a brother in the Lord.

Quartus has no significant postmodern redefinition; the principal point worth recovering is the dignity Scripture gives to the obscure faithful. The Spirit's preservation of an unknown believer's name and brotherhood stands against every culture, including our own, that measures worth by visibility and platform. In God's book of remembrance (Mal 3:16), the obscure who fear the LORD are not forgotten.
